title: Self-Mastery
tagline: Build habits, beat procrastination, and handle stress and setbacks.
description: The science of getting yourself to do what you said you would: habits that run on autopilot, beating procrastination, planning your week, setting goals that work, taming your phone, managing emotions, bouncing back from failure, and reviewing your life so you keep improving.

units.title: Build Habits That Stick
units.description: How habits form, how long it really takes, and how to design your surroundings so good habits are easy.

levels.title: How Habits Work
levels.summary: Cue, routine, reward, and the real timeline for a new habit.

steps.title: Autopilot mode
steps.body:
A **habit** is something you do automatically in response to a situation, without deciding each time. Brushing your teeth after breakfast. Checking your phone when you sit on the bus.

Habits form through a loop:
- **Cue:** a trigger, like a time, place, feeling or previous action
- **Routine:** the behavior
- **Reward:** something that feels good afterward

Repeat the loop in the same situation enough times and the cue starts to trigger the routine on its own.
steps.tip: Pick one habit you want to change and write its loop on a note: the cue, the routine, and the reward you get. Seeing the cue is the first step to changing it.

steps.prompt: Match each part of this habit to its role: 'When I get home from school, I grab chips and watch videos, and I feel relaxed.'
steps.hint: The cue comes first and triggers things. The routine is what you do. The reward is how you feel after.
steps.explain: The cue is the trigger, the routine is the action, and the reward is the good feeling that makes your brain want to repeat it. To change a habit, you can keep the cue and reward but swap the routine.

steps.title: It takes longer than 21 days
steps.body:
You may have heard it takes 21 days to form a habit. There is no good evidence for that number.

In a study at University College London (published in 2010), 96 people picked a new daily habit, like eating fruit at lunch or running before dinner. On average it took about **66 days** for the behavior to become automatic. But the range was huge: from **18 to 254 days** (the longest is an estimate, since the study only lasted 12 weeks). Simpler habits formed faster.

And the good news: **missing one day did not ruin the process.**
steps.tip: When you start a new habit, mark a date about 10 weeks out in your calendar. Judge how it is going then, not after the first week or two.

source.label: Lally et al. (2010), How are habits formed, European Journal of Social Psychology

steps.prompt: If you miss one day of a new habit, you have broken the streak and basically need to start over.
steps.explain: In the UCL study, missing a single day had little effect on habit formation. The danger is letting one missed day turn into a week. The rule many people use: never miss twice in a row.

steps.prompt: In the UCL habit study, about how long did it typically take for a new daily behavior to become automatic?
options: 7 days
21 days
66 days
1 year for everyone
steps.explain: About 66 days was typical (the median), with a range from 18 to 254 days. The popular '21 days' is a myth. Expect a couple of months for a habit that sticks, and longer for harder habits.

steps.title: Swap the routine
steps.body:
Bad habits are hard to delete because the cue and reward are still there. It is often easier to **replace the routine** while keeping cue and reward:

- Cue: bored on the bus. Old routine: scroll. Reward: stimulation. New routine: a podcast or a language app.
- Cue: stressed after work. Old routine: snacking. Reward: relief. New routine: a 10-minute walk or a call with a friend.

Ask: **what reward is this habit really giving me?**
steps.tip: Next time you notice a habit you want to drop, write down what you were feeling right before it. Then pick one healthier routine that gives you that same reward.

steps.prompt: You've noticed you reach for your phone the second you wake up and end up scrolling for 40 minutes. You want to change this. What's the most realistic plan?

options.text: Charge the phone across the room overnight, put a book or your workout clothes next to the bed, and use an alarm clock.
options.feedback: You change the cue (phone in reach) and make a new routine easy. This works better than trying to resist a phone that's on your pillow.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll just have more willpower tomorrow.
options.feedback: The cue and setup are unchanged. Relying on willpower at 6 a.m. rarely works.

options.text: Delete every app forever.
options.feedback: Possible, but extreme changes are hard to keep. Start by changing the setup.

options.text: Feel guilty every morning so you'll eventually stop.
options.feedback: Guilt tends to add stress, not change behavior. Change the situation instead.

steps.explain: Change the cue and make the new routine the easy option. Your setup beats your willpower.

steps.prompt: Which statements about habits are supported by research? Select all that apply.
options: Simple habits tend to become automatic faster than complex ones
It takes exactly 21 days to form any habit
Repeating a behavior in the same context helps it become automatic
Missing one day ruins habit formation
Habit formation time varies a lot between people and habits
steps.explain: Simple habits, consistent context and wide variation are all supported. The 21-day rule and the one-miss-ruins-it idea are not.

steps.prompt: Pick one habit you want to build or change. Write its cue, routine and reward. If changing a bad habit, what new routine could give the same reward?

levels.title: Start Tiny, Stack, Bundle
levels.summary: Make new habits so easy you can't say no, and attach them to things you already do.

steps.title: Start ridiculously small
steps.body:
The most common habit mistake: starting too big. '1 hour at the gym every day' fails by week two.

Start with a version so small it feels silly:
- 1 push-up
- Read 1 page
- Put on running shoes and step outside
- Floss 1 tooth

The goal at first is to **show up every day** so the cue-routine link forms. Doing more is a bonus. You can grow it once it's automatic.
steps.tip: Shrink your next new habit until it takes under two minutes, like one push-up or one page. Do that tiny version every day for two weeks before adding more.

steps.title: Habit stacking
steps.body:
**Habit stacking** attaches a new habit to one you already do every day. The existing habit becomes the cue.

Formula: **'After I [current habit], I will [new habit].'**

- After I pour my morning coffee, I will write my top task for the day.
- After I brush my teeth at night, I will set out tomorrow's clothes.
- After I sit down on the bus, I will do 5 minutes of language practice.

The more specific and reliable the anchor, the better.
steps.tip: Write one stack on a sticky note and put it where the anchor habit happens, like 'After I start the coffee, I write my top task' on the coffee maker.

steps.prompt: Which is the strongest habit stack?
options: 'Sometime in the evening, I'll stretch.'
'After I take off my shoes when I get home, I will do 5 minutes of stretching on the living room rug.'
'I'll stretch more this month.'
'When I feel like it, I'll stretch.'
steps.explain: It ties the new habit to a specific, daily action, names the place and the amount. The others have no clear cue.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for building a new habit in order.
steps.hint: Choose, shrink, attach, repeat, then grow. Growing comes only after the habit is automatic.
items: Pick one habit you want
Shrink it to a 2-minute version
Attach it to an existing daily habit
Do it every day, even the tiny version
Grow it gradually once it feels automatic
steps.explain: One habit, made tiny, anchored to a cue, repeated daily, then expanded. Trying to grow it before it's automatic is the usual way habits collapse.

steps.title: Temptation bundling
steps.body:
Researcher Katy Milkman tested a trick: only let yourself enjoy something you love **while** doing something you should do.

In her study, people got gripping audiobooks they could only listen to at the gym. At first they went to the gym up to **51% more** often than a control group, though the boost faded over the following weeks.

Examples:
- Favorite podcast only while cleaning or walking
- Fancy coffee only while doing homework
- A show you love only on the treadmill
steps.tip: Choose one podcast, playlist or show you love and save it only for a chore you avoid, like folding laundry or walking. Keep it off-limits the rest of the time.

source.label: Milkman, Minson and Volpp (2014), Management Science

steps.prompt: Match each example to the technique it uses.
steps.hint: Stacking ties to an existing habit. Bundling pairs a treat with a chore. Tiny means a very small start. Easy means less effort to begin.
pairs: 'After I start the dishwasher, I'll pack my lunch for tomorrow.'
'I only watch my favorite show while folding laundry.'
'I'll write just one sentence of my essay each day to start.'
'I sleep in my gym clothes so I can run right away.'
steps.explain: Stacking uses an existing cue, bundling pairs a treat with a chore, starting tiny lowers the bar, and making it easy removes steps.

steps.prompt: The best way to start a habit is with an ambitious goal, so you see big results fast and stay motivated.
steps.explain: Big starts often feel great for a few days and then collapse when life gets busy. Small, consistent actions build the cue-routine link. Results grow as you scale up.

steps.prompt: You want to start reading more. You've tried '30 minutes every night' twice and quit both times. What's a better plan?

options.text: 'After I get into bed, I'll read 2 pages.' Keep the book on your pillow, and keep the phone charging across the room.
options.feedback: Tiny, stacked onto a reliable cue, and the environment makes it easy. Most nights you'll read more than 2 pages anyway.

options.text: Try 60 minutes a night to really commit this time.
options.feedback: Raising the bar after failing twice makes a third failure more likely.

options.text: Wait until summer when you'll have more time.
options.feedback: Waiting for perfect conditions usually means never starting.

options.text: Buy 10 new books for motivation.
options.feedback: New books are fun, but they don't solve the cue and routine problem.

steps.explain: Shrink the habit, anchor it to a cue, and set up your environment. Consistency first, amount later.

steps.prompt: Write one habit stack for this week, using the formula 'After I ___, I will ___ (tiny version).'

levels.title: Design Your Environment
levels.summary: People with great self-control mostly avoid temptation instead of resisting it.

steps.title: Self-control is mostly setup
steps.body:
You might picture disciplined people as constantly resisting temptation. Research suggests otherwise.

In a study that pinged people throughout the day, those with high self-control reported **weaker** temptations and less inner conflict, and they actually resisted *less* often, not more. Other research suggests they set up their lives to avoid temptation.

In other words: disciplined people often don't win more fights with temptation. **They have fewer fights.**
steps.tip: Think of your biggest daily temptation and change one thing so you meet it less often, like a different route home, fewer snacks in the house, or a muted group chat.

source.label: Hofmann et al. (2012), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.title: Add friction, remove friction
steps.body:
Small amounts of effort change behavior a lot.

**Make good habits easier** (remove friction):
- Water bottle on your desk
- Guitar on a stand, not in its case
- Gym bag packed by the door

**Make bad habits harder** (add friction):
- Log out of social apps after each use
- Snacks in a high cabinet or not in the house
- Game controller in a drawer in another room
- Phone charging outside your bedroom
steps.tip: Tonight, charge your phone across the room or outside your bedroom, and put a book or alarm clock by your bed instead.

steps.prompt: Which changes add friction to a bad habit? Select all that apply.
options: Moving social media apps off your home screen into a folder
Keeping chips on the kitchen counter
Logging out of a shopping site so you have to re-enter your card
Turning on all notifications
Leaving your phone in another room while studying
steps.explain: Each one adds a step or distance between you and the habit. Chips on the counter and notifications remove friction from habits you're trying to cut.

steps.prompt: People with strong self-control mainly succeed by resisting temptations more often than other people.
steps.explain: Studies suggest people high in self-control experience fewer temptations, largely because they avoid situations and set up routines that keep temptation out of reach.

steps.prompt: You want to stop spending money on takeout. You spend about $60 a week on it, mostly on weeknights when you're tired. What change will help most?

options.text: Delete the delivery apps, and on Sunday make or buy easy dinners for 3 weeknights so a quick option is already at home.
options.feedback: You add friction to the bad habit and remove friction from the good one, exactly when you're tired.

options.text: Keep the apps but promise to be stronger.
options.feedback: Tired weeknight you will lose to one-tap ordering most of the time.

options.text: Feel bad every time you order.
options.feedback: Guilt doesn't change the setup. Changing the setup changes the behavior.

options.text: Order more expensive food so you'll feel the cost.
options.feedback: This just costs more. Make the alternative easier instead.

steps.explain: Plan for your tired self: make the better option the easiest one available at the moment of temptation.

steps.prompt: If cutting delivery saves you $40 a week, how many dollars is that over a 52-week year?
steps.hint: Multiply the weekly savings by the number of weeks in the year.
steps.explain: $40 x 52 = $2,080. Small environment changes can add up to real money.

steps.prompt: Order these steps for redesigning your environment around a habit.
steps.hint: You need to know when and where the habit happens before you can change that place.
items: Pick the habit you want to change
Notice when and where it happens
Add friction to the bad option in that place
Make the good option visible and easy there
Check in after a week and adjust
steps.explain: Find the moment, change the setup at that moment, then test and adjust.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Disciplined people mostly avoid temptation rather than resist it.
- Add friction to bad habits: distance, extra steps, logging out.
- Remove friction from good habits: put them in sight and ready to go.
- Design for your tired, stressed self, not your motivated self.

**This week:** make one friction change for a bad habit and one for a good habit. Write down what happens.

units.title: Get Things Done
units.description: Beat procrastination, plan your week, and set goals you actually reach.

levels.title: Beating Procrastination
levels.summary: Procrastination is about mood, not laziness. Here's how to start anyway.

steps.title: It's a feelings problem
steps.body:
Procrastination is not simply laziness or bad time management. Researchers describe it as **short-term mood repair**: a task makes you feel bored, anxious, confused or overwhelmed, so you do something that feels better right now.

That is why procrastinators often aren't relaxing. They are cleaning, scrolling, or doing easier tasks, anything to escape the bad feeling of the hard one.

So the fix starts with the feeling: **make starting feel less bad.**
steps.tip: When you notice yourself avoiding a task, ask: 'What feeling am I trying to escape?' Write the one-word answer down, then do the smallest first step.

source.label: Sirois and Pychyl (2013), Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation, Social and Personality Psychology Compass

steps.prompt: Procrastination is mainly caused by laziness.
steps.explain: Most procrastinators are busy doing other things. Research links procrastination to avoiding unpleasant feelings about a task, plus factors like how far away the deadline is and how much you value the task.

steps.title: Five ways to start
steps.body:
- **The 5-minute start:** 'I'll just work for 5 minutes.' Starting is the hardest part; often you keep going.
- **Make the first step tiny and specific:** not 'write essay' but 'open the doc and write the title.'
- **Name the feeling:** 'I'm avoiding this because I'm afraid it'll be bad.' Naming it often shrinks it.
- **Lower the bar:** give yourself permission for a bad first draft.
- **Remove escape routes:** phone in another room, one tab open.
steps.tip: Set a 5-minute timer on your phone and start the task you are avoiding. When it rings, you are allowed to stop. Most of the time you won't.

steps.prompt: Match each procrastination feeling to a good fix.
pairs: 'I don't even know where to start.'
Write down the very first tiny step
Pair it with music or a treat, or set a 25-minute timer
steps.explain: Different feelings need different fixes. Confusion needs a first step, perfectionism needs permission, boredom needs a bundle or a timer, and overwhelm needs a smaller start.

steps.title: Forgive yourself
steps.body:
It sounds backwards, but beating yourself up makes procrastination worse. Guilt adds more bad feeling to the task, so you want to avoid it even more.

In a study of college students, those who **forgave themselves** for procrastinating on studying for a first exam procrastinated **less** when studying for the next one.

Try: 'I put that off. That's human. What's one small step I can do now?'
steps.tip: After you put something off, say one kind sentence to yourself, like 'That's human,' and then name one small step you can take in the next hour.

source.label: Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett (2010), Personality and Individual Differences

steps.prompt: It's Sunday afternoon. You have a scholarship essay due Wednesday and you've avoided it all weekend. You feel a knot in your stomach every time you think of it. What do you do?

options.text: Say to yourself, 'I'm avoiding this because I'm nervous it won't be good enough.' Then set a 10-minute timer and just write a messy list of ideas.
options.feedback: You name the feeling, lower the bar, and make the start tiny and time-limited. Ten minutes in, it will probably feel much less scary.

options.text: Tell yourself you work better under pressure and wait until Tuesday night.
options.feedback: Many people believe this, but rushed work is usually worse, and the knot in your stomach stays all week.

options.text: Clean your whole room first so you can focus.
options.feedback: A classic procrastination move: a productive-looking escape.

options.text: Tell yourself you're hopeless and should just give up.
options.feedback: Self-criticism adds bad feelings to the task, which makes avoiding it more tempting.

steps.explain: Name the feeling, be kind to yourself, and make the first step tiny and time-boxed.

steps.prompt: Which are good ways to start a task you're dreading? Select all that apply.
options: Commit to working for just 5 minutes
Wait until you feel motivated
Write down the very first physical action
Tell yourself your first draft is allowed to be bad
Reorganize your desk first to set the mood
steps.explain: Short starts, concrete first actions and a lower bar make starting feel less bad. Waiting for motivation and pre-task 'prep' usually delay you further.

steps.prompt: What's one task you've been putting off? What feeling is behind it? What's the tiniest first step, and when will you do 5 minutes of it this week?
steps.placeholder: Task: ... Feeling: ... First tiny step: ... When: ...

levels.title: Plan Your Week
levels.summary: Weekly planning, time blocking and sorting what's urgent from what's important.

steps.title: Where does the time go?
steps.body:
Everyone gets 168 hours a week. Most people have no clear picture of where theirs go, so the important things get whatever's left over.

A **weekly plan** fixes this. Once a week (Sunday works for many), spend 15-20 minutes:
1. Look at your calendar and deadlines.
2. Pick your top 3 priorities for the week.
3. Block time for them **first**.
4. Fit everything else around them.
steps.tip: Set a repeating Sunday reminder called 'Plan my week' for 15 minutes. Use it to put your top 3 priorities into your calendar before anything else.

steps.prompt: A week has 168 hours. Say you sleep 56 hours a week (8 a night), spend 40 hours at school or work, and spend 21 hours on meals, getting ready and commuting (3 a day). How many hours are left?
steps.hint: Add up the three blocks of time, then subtract that total from 168.
steps.explain: Sleep: 8 x 7 = 56. Meals and travel: 3 x 7 = 21. 168 - 56 - 40 - 21 = 51 hours. That's a lot of time, which is why planning where it goes matters.

steps.title: Urgent vs important
steps.body:
The **Eisenhower matrix** sorts tasks by two questions: Is it **urgent** (needs attention now)? Is it **important** (matters for your goals)?

- **Urgent + important:** do it now (a paper due tomorrow).
- **Important, not urgent:** schedule it (studying for next month's exam, exercise, building skills).
- **Urgent, not important:** keep it short or hand it off (most notifications, some requests).
- **Neither:** drop it (mindless scrolling).

Studies found people often pick tasks that merely *feel* urgent over ones with bigger payoffs. The important-not-urgent box is where most progress happens.
steps.tip: Each morning, before you check messages, pick one important-but-not-urgent task and do 20 minutes of it first.

source.label: Zhu, Yang and Hsee (2018), The mere urgency effect, Journal of Consumer Research

steps.prompt: Sort each task into the right Eisenhower box.
steps.hint: Ask two questions for each task: does it need attention now, and does it matter for my goals?
pairs: Studying for the SAT that's 2 months away
Replying to a group chat about a meme
Not urgent, not important: skip or later
Filling out a job application due tonight
Urgent and important: do it now
A classmate asking you to proofread their essay right now
Urgent, less important to you: keep it short or say later
steps.explain: The SAT prep is easy to push off because it isn't urgent, but it matters most for your future. Scheduling it is how it actually gets done.

steps.title: Time blocking
steps.body:
**Time blocking** means giving each important task a specific slot in your calendar, like an appointment.

- 'Tuesday 4:00-5:00: bio lab report'
- 'Thursday 7:00-7:45: run'

Tips:
- Put hard work in your best-focus time.
- Leave buffer time; things take longer than planned.
- If a block gets missed, move it, don't delete it.
- Keep some unplanned time. A schedule with zero gaps breaks on the first surprise.
steps.tip: Put your next study or practice session in your phone calendar with a start and end time and an alert 10 minutes before. Treat it like a real appointment.

steps.prompt: Put a weekly planning session in order.
items: Review last week: what got done, what didn't
Check your calendar and deadlines for the coming week
Choose your top 3 priorities
Block time for those priorities first
Fit smaller tasks and errands around them
steps.explain: Review, look ahead, prioritize, protect time for the big things, then fill in the rest.

steps.prompt: Your week includes: a work shift Tuesday and Thursday, a big history project due Friday, a dentist appointment Wednesday, and you want to work out 3 times. It's Sunday night. What's the best plan?

options.text: Block 2 history project sessions on Monday and Wednesday plus a final check Thursday night, put workouts on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, and add the shifts and dentist to the calendar.
options.feedback: The big project gets protected time early with a buffer before Friday, and workouts fit around fixed commitments.

options.text: Work on the project Thursday night after your shift since it's due Friday.
options.feedback: That leaves one tired evening for a big project with no buffer if anything goes wrong.

options.text: Don't plan; just see how the week goes.
options.feedback: Without a plan, urgent things crowd out important ones and the project ends up last-minute.

options.text: Skip workouts this week to focus on the project.
options.feedback: Sometimes needed, but here there's room for both with a little planning.

steps.explain: Put fixed commitments in first, protect early blocks for the big priority, and fit the rest around them.

steps.prompt: A good schedule fills every hour of the day so no time is wasted.
steps.explain: Packed schedules fall apart at the first delay, and the planning fallacy means tasks usually run long. Leave buffers and some free time.

steps.prompt: This Sunday (or today), do a 15-minute weekly plan. What are your top 3 priorities, and when are they blocked?

levels.title: Goals That Work
levels.summary: Specific goals, if-then plans, and imagining obstacles in advance.

steps.title: Specific beats 'do your best'
steps.body:
Decades of research by psychologists Edwin Locke and Gary Latham found that **specific, challenging goals** usually lead to better performance than vague goals like 'do your best.'

- Vague: 'Get in shape.'
- Specific: 'Run a 5K without stopping by June 1.'
- Vague: 'Save money.'
- Specific: 'Save $1,200 for a car fund by December.'

A specific goal tells you what to do and lets you see progress.
steps.tip: Rewrite one vague goal you have so it includes a number and a date, like 'Run 5K without stopping by June 1.' Write it where you will see it daily.

source.label: Locke and Latham (2002), Building a practically useful theory of goal setting, American Psychologist

steps.prompt: Which goals are specific enough to track? Select all that apply.
options: 'Get better at Spanish.'
'Complete 2 Spanish lessons a day and hold a 5-minute conversation by May.'
'Read more.'
'Read 12 books this year, about 1 a month.'
'Save $50 from each paycheck into savings.'
steps.explain: Each has a clear amount and timeframe, so you know if you're on track. 'Get better' and 'read more' give you nothing to measure.

steps.title: If-then plans
steps.body:
Goals say *what* you want. **Implementation intentions** say exactly *when, where and how* you'll act:

**'If (or when) [situation], then I will [action].'**

- 'When I get home from school on Mondays and Wednesdays, I will do 30 minutes of SAT practice at the kitchen table.'
- 'If someone offers me a vape, then I will say no thanks and change the subject.'

A review of 94 studies found if-then plans had a **medium-to-large effect** on actually reaching goals.
steps.tip: For your most important goal, write one sentence: 'When [day, time, place], I will [action].' Put it in your phone as a repeating reminder at that time.

source.label: Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Which is the best implementation intention for the goal 'Work out more'?
options: 'I will work out more this month.'
'I'll try to go to the gym when I can.'
'When I finish my Tuesday and Thursday shifts at 5 p.m., I will drive straight to the gym for 30 minutes.'
'I really want to get stronger.'
steps.explain: It names the situation (after Tuesday and Thursday shifts), the place and the action. The others are intentions without a trigger.

steps.title: Plan for the obstacle
steps.body:
Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen found that just fantasizing about success can **drain the energy** you need to act. A better method, called **WOOP**:

- **Wish:** what you want
- **Outcome:** the best result, imagined vividly
- **Obstacle:** the main thing *inside you* that could get in the way (tiredness, phone, nerves)
- **Plan:** an if-then plan for that obstacle

'If I feel too tired to study after work, then I will do just 10 minutes of flashcards before I lie down.'
steps.tip: Before your next big goal, spend five minutes writing your WOOP: the wish, the best outcome, the main inner obstacle, and one if-then plan for it.

source.label: Kappes and Oettingen (2011), Positive fantasies about idealized futures sap energy, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Put the WOOP steps in order.
items: Wish: name what you want
Outcome: picture the best result
Obstacle: name what in you could get in the way
Plan: write an if-then plan for that obstacle
steps.explain: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan. The obstacle step is what makes it different from just positive thinking.

steps.prompt: You want to save $1,200 for a car in 6 months. You get paid every 2 weeks, so about 13 paychecks in 6 months. About how many dollars should you save per paycheck? (Round to the nearest whole dollar.)
steps.hint: Divide the total goal by the number of paychecks, then round.
steps.explain: $1,200 / 13 = about $92.31, so about $92 per paycheck. Breaking a big goal into a per-paycheck number makes it a concrete habit you can automate.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: 'My goal this year is to be healthier.' They've said this the past two years. What's the most useful thing to say?

options.text: 'What would healthier look like, specifically? Maybe pick one thing, like walking 20 minutes after dinner on weekdays, and plan for what usually gets in the way.'
options.feedback: You help make it specific, shrink it to one habit, and plan for obstacles: the three moves that make goals stick.

options.text: 'Just visualize yourself healthy every day.'
options.feedback: Fantasizing alone can lower effort. Pair it with obstacles and a plan.

options.text: 'You never stick to anything, so why bother?'
options.feedback: Discouraging and not true. The goal format is the problem, not your friend.

options.text: 'Great! Go big: diet, gym, sleep, everything at once.'
options.feedback: Changing everything at once usually collapses fast. One specific habit is more likely to stick.

steps.explain: Make it specific, make it a habit with a trigger, and plan for the obstacle.

steps.prompt: Do a WOOP for one goal this week: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, and an if-then Plan.
steps.placeholder: Wish: ... Outcome: ... Obstacle: ... Plan: If ..., then I will ...

units.title: Emotions and Resilience
units.description: Name and manage strong emotions, calm your body fast, and bounce back from failure.

levels.title: Name It to Tame It
levels.summary: Putting feelings into words reduces their intensity.

steps.title: Labels calm the alarm
steps.body:
When you're upset, it might seem like thinking about the feeling would make it worse. Research suggests the opposite.

In a 2007 brain-imaging study, people looked at angry or scared faces. When they **put a word to the emotion** ('angry'), activity in the amygdala, a brain area involved in alarm, went down compared with just looking.

This is called **affect labeling**. A simple version: 'I'm feeling anxious right now.'
steps.tip: When a strong feeling hits, pause and say to yourself, 'I'm feeling ___ right now.' Do it before you text, post or reply.

source.label: Lieberman et al. (2007), Psychological Science

steps.title: Get specific
steps.body:
'I feel bad' is a start, but more specific words help more. They tell you what you actually need.

- Instead of **bad**: disappointed, embarrassed, lonely, guilty, jealous, overwhelmed
- Instead of **mad**: irritated, betrayed, frustrated, resentful
- Instead of **stressed**: worried, rushed, unprepared, pressured

Psychologists call this **emotional granularity**. People who can describe emotions more precisely tend to handle them better.
steps.tip: Save a list of feeling words in your phone notes. When you feel 'bad' or 'stressed,' pick the most exact word from the list.

source.label: Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight (2015), Unpacking emotion differentiation, Current Directions in Psychological Science

steps.prompt: Match each situation to the most specific feeling word.
pairs: Your friends went to a movie without inviting you
You studied hard but still failed the quiz
You have three deadlines tomorrow and a shift tonight
You said something dumb in front of your crush
steps.explain: Specific words point to specific needs: being included, a new study plan, prioritizing tasks, or simply letting a moment pass.

steps.prompt: Putting your feelings into words usually makes them more intense.
steps.hint: Think about what happened in the amygdala when people put a word to the emotion.
steps.explain: Studies on affect labeling suggest naming an emotion often reduces its intensity. It's different from dwelling on it for hours, which can make things worse.

steps.title: Venting is not the same
steps.body:
Naming a feeling is helpful. **Venting** anger by yelling, punching a pillow or ranting tends to do the opposite.

In a 2002 experiment, people who were made angry and then hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them became **more** aggressive afterward than people who did nothing.

Better options: name it, slow your breathing, take a walk, and talk it through once you're calmer.
steps.tip: When you are angry, write the rant in your notes app instead of sending it. Wait at least an hour, then decide what, if anything, to send.

source.label: Bushman (2002), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

steps.prompt: Your coach benches you without explanation. You're furious and about to text your teammate a long rant. What's the best first move?

options.text: Pause and name it to yourself: 'I'm angry and embarrassed.' Take a few slow breaths or a short walk. Then later ask the coach: 'Can you tell me what I need to work on to get back in?'
options.feedback: Naming the feeling cools it down, and asking the coach later turns it into something you can act on.

options.text: Send the rant now while it's fresh.
options.feedback: Messages sent in anger often get forwarded or regretted. Venting can also keep the anger going.

options.text: Pretend you don't care and push it down.
options.feedback: Suppressing emotions tends to keep them around and can make you seem cold. Naming them works better.

options.text: Quit the team.
options.feedback: A big, permanent decision made in the heat of the moment. Wait until you're calm.

steps.explain: Name the feeling, cool down your body, and then act on the problem when you're calm.

steps.prompt: Which are helpful ways to handle a strong feeling? Select all that apply.
options: Saying or writing what you feel: 'I'm really frustrated.'
Punching a wall to get it out
Taking a short walk
Making a big decision right away so it's over
Talking it through with someone once you're calmer
steps.explain: Naming, moving and talking once calm all help. Venting physically and deciding in the heat of the moment usually make things worse.

steps.prompt: For the next 3 days, once a day, write one specific word for what you're feeling and why. What patterns do you notice?

levels.title: Reframe and Breathe
levels.summary: Change the story you tell yourself, and calm your body in minutes.

steps.title: Reframing
steps.body:
How you feel about an event depends a lot on how you interpret it. **Cognitive reappraisal**, or reframing, means deliberately looking for another accurate way to see the situation.

- Event: your friend didn't reply all day.
- Story A: 'They're mad at me.' (anxious)
- Story B: 'They're probably busy. They have a big test this week.' (calm)

Reframing is not lying to yourself. It's checking whether your first story is the only possible one. Research links habitual reappraisal with better emotional well-being.
steps.tip: Next time a text or comment upsets you, write down two other explanations that could also be true before you respond.

source.label: Gross and John (2003), Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.prompt: You get a C on a test you studied for. Which thought is a helpful reframe?
options: 'I'm stupid. I'll never get this.'
'This shows me which topics I don't know yet. I'll check what I missed and change how I study.'
'Tests don't matter anyway.'
'Everything is fine, I'm sure the teacher made a mistake.'
steps.explain: It's realistic and points to action. The first is harsh and permanent, the third dismisses something you care about, and the fourth avoids reality.

steps.title: Three reframing questions
steps.body:
When a thought makes you feel terrible, try:

1. **What's another explanation?** Is there a less awful reason this could have happened?
2. **What would I tell a friend?** We're usually kinder and more reasonable with others.
3. **Will this matter in a year?** Sometimes yes, often less than it feels.

The goal isn't to feel great about everything. It's to see the situation as clearly as possible.
steps.tip: When a thought is dragging you down, ask: 'What would I tell a friend who said this?' Then say that same thing to yourself.

steps.title: Calm your body: cyclic sighing
steps.body:
Breathing changes your body's stress response quickly. In a 2023 Stanford study, people did 5 minutes of breathing exercises daily for a month. **Cyclic sighing** improved mood more than mindfulness meditation did.

How to do it:
1. Inhale through your nose.
2. Take a second short inhale on top to fill your lungs.
3. Breathe out slowly through your mouth, longer than the inhales.
4. Repeat for 1 to 5 minutes.

It works fast: a few cycles can take the edge off before a test or a hard conversation.
steps.tip: Do two minutes of cyclic sighing right before your next test, game or hard conversation: two inhales through the nose, then one long exhale through the mouth.

source.label: Balban et al. (2023), Cell Reports Medicine

steps.prompt: Put one round of cyclic sighing in order.
items: Inhale through your nose
Take a second short inhale to fully fill your lungs
Exhale slowly through your mouth, longer than the inhales
Repeat for a few minutes
steps.explain: Double inhale, long exhale, repeat. The long exhale is the key part for calming down.

steps.prompt: In the 2023 Stanford study, the breathing practices only helped if people did them for at least an hour a day.
steps.hint: Recall how long the daily breathing sessions were in the Stanford study.
steps.explain: Participants did just 5 minutes a day. Short, regular practice was enough to see benefits in mood over the month.

steps.prompt: You're about to walk into a job interview. Your heart is pounding and you're thinking, 'I'm going to mess this up.' What's the best approach?

options.text: Do a few rounds of cyclic sighing, then reframe: 'My body is getting ready. I'm excited about this job. I've prepared, and one interview won't decide my whole future.'
options.feedback: You calm your body and change the story at the same time. Both are fast and backed by research.

options.text: Tell yourself 'Just calm down' over and over.
options.feedback: Ordering yourself to calm down rarely works. Breathing and reframing give your brain something concrete.

options.text: Scroll on your phone to distract yourself.
options.feedback: Distraction can help a little, but you may walk in scattered. A minute of breathing is more reliable.

options.text: Leave before it starts.
options.feedback: Avoiding the situation relieves anxiety short-term but makes it stronger next time.

steps.explain: Body first (breathing), then mind (a realistic, hopeful reframe).

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Your first story about an event isn't the only one. Look for another accurate interpretation.
- Ask: another explanation? What would I tell a friend? Will it matter in a year?
- Cyclic sighing (double inhale, long exhale) for a few minutes can calm your body.
- If strong feelings like sadness or anxiety last for weeks or get in the way of daily life, talk to a doctor, counselor or trusted adult. In the US you can call or text 988 any time.

**This week:** practice cyclic sighing for 2 minutes a day.

levels.title: Bouncing Back from Failure
levels.summary: Self-compassion, learning from mistakes, and why setbacks are normal.

steps.title: Failure is part of the process
steps.body:
Everyone fails: athletes miss shots, entrepreneurs see businesses fail, scientists run experiments that don't work. What differs is what happens next.

**Resilience** is not never getting knocked down. It's getting back up and adjusting. It's a set of skills you can practice:
- Treating yourself kindly after a setback
- Learning what went wrong
- Leaning on other people
- Taking the next small step
steps.tip: After a setback, do one small next step within 24 hours, like sending one more application or booking one more practice. It keeps you moving.

steps.title: Self-compassion helps you improve
steps.body:
Some people think being hard on themselves is what keeps them motivated. Research suggests the opposite.

In a 2012 study, students who failed a hard test and were then encouraged to be **kind and understanding toward themselves** studied **longer** for a second test than students who got a self-esteem boost or a pleasant distraction.

Self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook. It's talking to yourself like a good coach would: honest, but on your side.
steps.tip: After you fail at something, write yourself a short note the way a good coach would: what went wrong, what you will try next, and one thing you did well.

source.label: Breines and Chen (2012), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

steps.prompt: Being harsh with yourself after a failure is the best way to make sure you work harder next time.
steps.explain: In studies, self-compassion after failure led to more effort to improve, not less. Harsh self-criticism tends to increase fear of failure, which leads to avoidance.

steps.prompt: Match each self-talk example to its type.
steps.hint: Self-compassion is honest and kind. Avoidance pretends it didn't matter. Denial blames everyone else.
pairs: 'I'm such an idiot. I ruin everything.'
'That stung. Lots of people miss on their first try. What can I change?'
'Whatever, it doesn't matter, I didn't even care.'
'I'm amazing, the judges were just wrong.'
steps.explain: Self-compassion admits the failure, treats it as normal, and looks forward. The others either attack you, pretend you don't care, or dodge reality.

steps.title: After-action review
steps.body:
The US Army and many companies use a quick **after-action review** after anything important, good or bad:

1. What was supposed to happen?
2. What actually happened?
3. Why was there a difference?
4. What will I do differently next time?

It turns 'I failed' into 'I learned.' It also works for wins: knowing *why* something worked helps you repeat it.
steps.tip: After your next game, test or shift, answer the four after-action questions in your notes app. It takes about five minutes.

source.label: Wharton Executive Education (2012), After-action reviews

steps.prompt: Put the after-action review questions in order.
steps.hint: Start with the plan, then compare it with reality, then explain the gap, then decide what to change.
items: What was supposed to happen?
What actually happened?
Why was there a difference?
What will I do differently next time?
steps.explain: Plan vs reality, then why, then what next. It keeps the focus on learning, not blame.

steps.prompt: You applied to 8 part-time jobs and got rejected by all of them. You feel like giving up. What's the most resilient response?

options.text: Allow yourself to feel disappointed, then ask someone you trust to look over your resume and practice an interview with you, and apply to 5 more with those changes.
options.feedback: You acknowledge the feeling, get outside feedback on what to fix, and take the next step. That's resilience in action.

options.text: 'Nobody wants to hire me. I'll stop trying.'
options.feedback: A permanent, global conclusion from a temporary setback. Job searches often take many applications.

options.text: Keep sending the exact same application to 50 more places.
options.feedback: Persistence is good, but without adjusting, you may get the same result.

options.text: Pretend you didn't really want a job anyway.
options.feedback: Protecting your feelings by pretending not to care means you also stop trying.

steps.explain: Feel it, learn from it with help, adjust, and try again.

steps.prompt: Which thoughts show a resilient mindset? Select all that apply.
options: 'This is hard right now, but it won't last forever.'
'I always fail at everything.'
'What's one thing I can learn from this?'
'Who could help me with this?'
'If I fail once, I'm not cut out for it.'
steps.explain: Seeing setbacks as temporary, learning from them and asking for help are signs of resilience. 'Always' and 'not cut out for it' turn one setback into a permanent label.

steps.prompt: Think of a recent setback. Run an after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what you'll do next time. Then write one kind sentence to yourself about it.
steps.placeholder: Supposed to: ... Actually: ... Why: ... Next time: ... Kind sentence: ...

units.title: Focus, Discipline and Reflection
units.description: Take control of your phone, keep going when motivation fades, and review your life so you keep getting better.

levels.title: You vs Your Phone
levels.summary: Apps are designed to grab attention. Here's how to set limits that work.

steps.title: It's not a fair fight
steps.body:
Social media and many games are designed by large teams to keep you using them: endless feeds, autoplay, streaks, notifications and unpredictable rewards (you never know when the next good post will appear).

That doesn't make phones evil. But willpower alone is not a match for a product engineered to be hard to put down. You need **setup and limits**.
steps.tip: Turn off autoplay in your video and streaming apps' settings, so the next episode or video does not start on its own.

steps.prompt: Suppose you spend 3 hours a day on social media. How many hours is that in a 365-day year?
steps.hint: Multiply the hours per day by the days in a year.
steps.explain: 3 x 365 = 1,095 hours. That's more than 45 full days, or about the number of hours in 27 full-time work weeks.

steps.title: What happened when students cut back
steps.body:
In a 2018 University of Pennsylvania experiment, 143 college students were split into two groups. One group limited Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to **10 minutes per platform per day** (30 minutes total) for 3 weeks. The other used them as usual.

The limited group showed significant drops in **loneliness and depression** compared with the control group.

It was one study with college students, but it suggests cutting back, not quitting entirely, can make a difference.
steps.tip: Use your phone's app limits to cap each social app at a set time per day, like 15 minutes, for the next three weeks. Notice how you feel.

source.label: Hunt et al. (2018), Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology

steps.prompt: In the 2018 University of Pennsylvania study, students had to quit social media completely to see benefits.
steps.explain: They limited use to about 10 minutes per platform per day, about 30 minutes total, and still saw lower loneliness and depression compared with the control group.

steps.title: Phone setup that works
steps.body:
- **Notifications:** turn off everything except calls and messages from real people.
- **Home screen:** only tools (maps, calendar, camera). Move social apps into a folder off the first screen.
- **Screen time limits:** set daily app limits in your phone's settings.
- **Grayscale mode:** makes the screen less eye-catching. Some people find it cuts mindless use.
- **Phone-free zones:** bedroom, meals, focus blocks.
- **Log out** of the app you overuse, so opening it takes effort.
steps.tip: Open your phone's notification settings now and turn off alerts for every app that is not a real person messaging or calling you.

steps.prompt: Which phone changes add helpful friction? Select all that apply.
options: Turning off non-human notifications
Putting your most-used social app on the home screen dock
Setting a 30-minute daily limit on social apps
Charging the phone outside the bedroom
Turning on autoplay for videos
steps.explain: Fewer notifications, daily limits and distance all make mindless use harder. A prime home-screen spot and autoplay make it easier.

steps.prompt: You notice you check Instagram about 80 times a day, often without thinking. You don't want to quit, just get control. What's the best first step?

options.text: Turn off Instagram notifications, move it off your home screen, and set a daily limit of 30 minutes in your phone settings. Check your screen time after one week.
options.feedback: Adds friction, sets a clear limit, and builds in a check. It's specific and doesn't require quitting.

options.text: Delete the app forever and tell everyone you're done.
options.feedback: Fine if it works for you, but all-or-nothing changes often bounce back. A clear limit may last longer.

options.text: Try to check it less, starting tomorrow.
options.feedback: No plan and no change to the setup. The cues are all still there.

options.text: Unfollow a few accounts.
options.feedback: Can improve your feed, but it doesn't address how often you check.

steps.explain: Reduce cues, set a specific limit, and measure. Small setup changes beat good intentions.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Apps are designed to be hard to put down. Willpower alone isn't enough.
- Cutting back, not quitting, improved well-being in at least one experiment.
- Turn off non-human notifications, hide apps, set limits, and keep phones out of the bedroom.
- Check your screen time weekly.

**This week:** look at your screen time, pick your top app, and set a daily limit about 30% below your current average.

levels.title: Discipline Without Motivation
levels.summary: Motivation comes and goes. Systems keep you going anyway.

steps.title: Motivation follows action
steps.body:
Many people wait to feel motivated before starting. But motivation is a feeling, and feelings come and go.

Often it works the other way: **starting creates motivation**. Ten minutes into a workout or an essay, you often feel more like continuing than you did before.

Disciplined people aren't always motivated. They have **systems** that get them started anyway: fixed times, small starts, environments that make it easy, and commitments to other people.
steps.tip: On low-energy days, promise yourself only the first 10 minutes of the task. Starting is the hard part, and you can stop after that if you want.

steps.title: Myth: willpower is a battery
steps.body:
For years, a popular idea said self-control is like a battery that drains with use (called **ego depletion**). If you resist cookies, you'll have less willpower left for homework.

When 23 labs repeated a standard ego depletion experiment with over 2,000 people in 2016, the effect was **close to zero**. Later large tests also found the effect was tiny at most.

So don't assume you've 'used up' your willpower. Tiredness and stress are real, but there's no fixed tank that resisting one cookie drains.

source.label: Hagger et al. (2016), multilab replication, Perspectives on Psychological Science

steps.prompt: Large replication studies strongly confirmed that willpower runs out like a battery after you use it.
steps.explain: A 23-lab replication in 2016 found an effect close to zero. The battery idea is popular but not well supported. Rest and routines still matter, but don't treat willpower as a fuel tank.

steps.title: Myth: the marshmallow test is destiny
steps.body:
In famous studies from the 1960s-70s, kids who waited longer for a second marshmallow had better outcomes later. It became a symbol of 'self-control decides your future.'

A larger, more diverse 2018 follow-up found the link was **about half as strong**, and it shrank by about two-thirds once researchers accounted for family background and early abilities.

The takeaway: self-control matters, but it isn't fixed at age 4, and circumstances play a big role.

source.label: Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018), Revisiting the marshmallow test, Psychological Science

steps.prompt: Match each discipline tool to an example.
steps.hint: A commitment device puts something at stake if you skip. A minimum version is the smallest acceptable effort.
pairs: Study every weekday at 4 p.m. no matter how you feel
Text a friend after each workout
On bad days, just do 10 push-ups instead of a full workout
Pay a friend $5 every time you skip your planned study session
steps.explain: Schedules remove daily decisions, partners add social commitment, minimum versions keep the streak alive, and commitment devices make skipping cost something.

steps.prompt: You've been running 3 times a week for a month. Today it's cold, you're tired, and you really don't feel like it. What's the best move?

options.text: Do the minimum version: put on your shoes and go for just 10 minutes. If you feel better after, keep going; if not, you still kept the habit.
options.feedback: The minimum version protects the habit on bad days. Often you'll end up doing more once you start.

options.text: Skip it and plan to run twice tomorrow.
options.feedback: 'Double tomorrow' plans rarely happen and can make tomorrow feel dreaded.

options.text: Force yourself through a full hard run while miserable.
options.feedback: Sometimes fine, but if every bad day is torture, you'll start to dread the habit. A minimum version keeps it sustainable.

options.text: Decide you're not a runner after all.
options.feedback: One low-motivation day isn't evidence about who you are.

steps.explain: On low days, do the minimum. Showing up keeps the habit alive; intensity can wait for better days.

steps.prompt: Which strategies keep you going when motivation is low? Select all that apply.
options: Doing a 2-minute minimum version
Waiting until you feel inspired
Having a set time so you don't have to decide
Telling a friend your plan and checking in
Assuming you've run out of willpower for the day
steps.explain: Minimum versions, fixed times and accountability keep you moving without relying on feelings. Waiting for inspiration and the willpower battery story mostly give you reasons to stop.

steps.prompt: Pick one thing you want to do consistently. Write its fixed time, its minimum version for bad days, and one person you could check in with.

levels.title: Reflection Habits
levels.summary: A short weekly review that keeps you learning from your own life.

steps.title: Experience plus reflection
steps.body:
Experience alone doesn't always make you better. **Reflecting** on it does more.

Researchers at Harvard Business School found that workers in training who spent the last 15 minutes of the day writing about what they had learned scored about **23% higher** on their final training test than those who spent that time practicing more.

Reflection turns 'stuff that happened' into lessons you can use.
steps.tip: Before bed, write two lines in your notes app: one thing you learned today and one thing you would do differently.

source.label: Di Stefano, Gino, Pisano and Staats, Making experience count: the role of reflection in individual learning (working paper)

steps.title: A 15-minute weekly review
steps.body:
Once a week, maybe right before you plan the next week, answer:

1. **What went well?** Why?
2. **What didn't go well?** Why?
3. **What did I learn?**
4. **What's one thing I'll do differently next week?**
5. **What am I grateful for?**

Write the answers down. In a few months, you can look back and see real patterns in your energy, habits and moods.
steps.tip: Set a weekly reminder for the same time you plan your week, and keep your review answers in one notes file so you can scroll back and spot patterns.

steps.prompt: Put the weekly review steps in a sensible order.
items: Look back at your calendar and notes from the week
Write what went well and why
Write what didn't go well and why
Pick one change for next week
Plan next week's top 3 priorities
steps.explain: Review the facts, notice wins and misses, choose one change, then plan forward with that change in mind.

steps.prompt: Which weekly review answer is most useful?
options: 'This week was bad.'
'I skipped 3 of 4 workouts, every time on days I worked late. Next week I'll move workouts to mornings on work days.'
'I need to try harder.'
'Everything was fine I guess.'
steps.explain: It names a specific pattern (late work days), a cause, and a concrete change. Vague judgments don't tell you what to do differently.

steps.prompt: Reflection is only useful after something goes wrong.
steps.explain: Reviewing what went well tells you what to keep doing and why it worked. The US Army's after-action reviews and many workplace reviews cover successes as well as failures.

steps.prompt: Which make a reflection habit easier to stick with? Select all that apply.
options: Doing it at the same time each week
Keeping it short, like 10-15 minutes
Writing a 5-page essay every time
Pairing it with something you enjoy, like a favorite drink
Only doing it when you feel inspired
steps.explain: A fixed time, a short format and a pleasant pairing make it a habit. Long essays and waiting for inspiration make it easy to skip.

steps.prompt: You notice in your weekly review that you've felt drained every Monday for a month. What's the best next step?

options.text: Look for a pattern: check your Sunday nights. If you're staying up late on Sundays, try a set Sunday bedtime for two weeks and see if Mondays improve.
options.feedback: You use your notes to find a likely cause and run a small, testable experiment.

options.text: Accept that Mondays are just bad.
options.feedback: Maybe, but you have data that could help you find a fix.

options.text: Change everything in your routine at once.
options.feedback: If things improve, you won't know which change helped. Test one change at a time.

options.text: Stop doing weekly reviews since they make you notice bad stuff.
options.feedback: Noticing patterns is the point. It's how you fix them.

steps.explain: Treat patterns as clues, test one change, and check the results in a future review.

steps.prompt: Do your first weekly review now: what went well, what didn't, what you learned, one change for next week, and one thing you're grateful for. Then set a recurring reminder for the same time next week.
steps.placeholder: Went well: ... Didn't: ... Learned: ... One change: ... Grateful for: ...
